keywords: Render > Shader Nodes > Input Ambient Occlusion Node Outputs
text:
Color
   Ambient occlusion with color tint.
AO
   Ambient occlusion factor without color tint.
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/input/ao.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Attribute Node
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes > Input Attribute Node Attribute Node
text: The *Attribute* node allows you to retrieve attributes attached to an object or mesh.
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/input/attribute.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Attribute Node > Properties
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes > Input Attribute Node Properties
text:
Attribute Type
   Specifies the type of the attribute.
   The property value must be an integer, float, boolean, or a vector of 1 to 4 floats or ints; properties of other
   types are ignored. If a suitable property is not found, all sockets of the node, including *Alpha*, output 0.

   :Geometry:
      The attribute is associated with the geometry of the object, and its value varies from
      vertex to vertex, or within the volume of the object.

      Most geometry attributes are directly accessible through the various input nodes, except for these:

      Ocean Foam
         Gives a scalar defining where foam might appear when using
         an Ocean Modifier.
         This depends on the name you give this property.

Seealso:

         For a full list of options see `This Thread <https://blender.stackexchange.com/questions/14262#14267>`__
         on the Blender Stack Exchange.
   :Object:
      The attribute name specifies a custom property name,
      or an RNA path to a built-in property (like the single property driver variables).

      The values of attributes of this type are defined once per object. The name or path is looked up
      first in the object data-block, followed by the mesh data-block if not found.
      Custom properties have priority over built-in ones.

Tip:

         The color attribute will output the value of the Color field in
         the Viewport Display panel of
         the object, unless overridden by a custom property.
   :Instancer:
      Similar to *Object*, but the attribute is looked up in the instancer particle system settings,
      followed by Geometry Node instance attributes
      (searching from the innermost instancing layer to outer ones), and finally in the instancer object.
      If the current object is not instanced
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/input/attribute.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Attribute Node > Outputs
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes > Input Attribute Node Outputs
text:
Color
   RGB color interpolated from the attribute.
Vector
   XYZ vector interpolated from the attribute.
Factor
   Scalar value interpolated from the attribute.
Alpha
   Alpha channel of the attribute, when available. If the attribute has no alpha channel, generally defaults to 1.

Warning:

   Currently, only *View Layer* attributes are supported in shaders used for the World
   or Light Objects.
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/input/attribute.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Bevel Node
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes > Input Bevel Node Bevel Node
text:
Cycles Only

The Bevel shader node can be used for rendering rounded corners.
Like bump mapping, this does not modify the actual geometry, only the shading is affected.
Slight rounding on edges helps to capture specular highlights that you would also see in the real world.

Note that this is a very expensive shader, and may slow down renders
by 20% even if there is a lot of other complexity in the scene.
For that reason, we suggest to mainly use this for baking or
still frame renders where render time is not as much of an issue.
The bevel is a faster option when it works,
but sometimes fails on complex or messy geometry.

Note:

   **The Bevel node will not produce a valid result when:**

   - The object is either a Caustic caster
      or Caustic receiver while the scene
      contains an active Caustic caster,
      Caustic receiver, and
      Shadow Caustic Light.
   - index is active while using the OptiX rendering backend.
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/input/bevel.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Bevel Node > Inputs
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes > Input Bevel Node Inputs
text:
Radius
   Width of the bevel effect on edges.
Normal
   Normal to apply bevel on top of, to be combined with a bump
   for example. When not connected, uses the surface normal.
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/input/bevel.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Bevel Node > Properties
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes > Input Bevel Node Properties
text:
Samples
   Number of samples to take for each shader evaluation.
   More samples give more accurate results, but are also slower to render.
   The default value of 4 works well for most cases, with any noise resolved by using more AA samples.
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/input/bevel.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Camera Data Node
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes > Input Camera Data Node Camera Data Node
text:
The *Camera Data* node returns information about the shading point relative to the camera.
This could be used for example to change the shading
of objects further away from the camera, or make custom fog effects.
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/input/camera_data.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Camera Data Node > Outputs
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes > Input Camera Data Node Outputs
text:
View Vector
   A normalized vector, in camera space, from the camera to the shading point.
View Z Depth
   The distance each pixel is away from the camera.
View Distance
   Distance from the camera to the shading point.
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/input/camera_data.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Value Node
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes > Input > Constant Value Node Value Node
text: The *Value Node* is a simple node to input numerical values to other nodes in the tree.
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/input/constant/value.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Value Node > Example
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes > Input > Constant Value Node Example
text:
In the following example the *Value Node* is used to control multiple values at once,
this makes the node a useful organizational tool.

Tip:

   From this you can also make different values proportional to each other by adding
   a Math Node in between the different links.
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/input/constant/value.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Fresnel Node
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes > Input Fresnel Node Fresnel Node
text:
The *Fresnel* (or *Dielectric Fresnel*) node computes the proportion of light reflected
off a surface at a given viewing angle, based on the index of refraction (IOR).
At grazing angles, more light is reflected than at a direct view —
matching real-world behavior where windows and water appear more reflective at the edges.
The output weight ranges from 0.0 to 1.0 and is used as a blend factor in a *Mix Shader* node.

This node provides a direct IOR input, which determines the strength of the Fresnel effect.
For cases where adjusting the IOR is not critical or where a simpler 0.0–1.0 value range is preferred,
consider the *Fresnel* output of the Layer Weight Node,
which maps a *Blend* value of 0.5 to an IOR of 1.5 and offers a more convenient input range.

The most common use is mixing between two shaders — for example, a glossy refraction shader
and a glossy reflection shader to create glass, or a diffuse base shader and a glossy coating
shader to create plastic. At grazing angles the glossy coating or reflection dominates;
straight-on, the diffuse base or refraction shows through.
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/input/fresnel.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Fresnel Node > Inputs
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes > Input Fresnel Node Inputs
text:
IOR
   Index of refraction (IOR) of the material. Controls how strong the Fresnel
   effect appears. Common IOR values:

   - 1.00 : Air
   - 1.33 : Water
   - 1.50 : Typical glass / standard plastic
   - 1.52 : Window glass (float glass)
   - 1.77 : Sapphire
   - 2.42 : Diamond

   Higher values produce stronger reflection at edges.
   Lower values make the reflection visible over a wider range of viewing angles.
Normal
   Optional input for a bump or normal map. When connected, the surface angle
   at each point is modified by the bump/normal detail before computing the Fresnel weight.
   This makes the reflection pattern respond to surface texture, adding realism
   to materials with visible surface detail.
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/input/fresnel.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Fresnel Node > Outputs
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes > Input Fresnel Node Outputs
text:
Factor
   Fresnel weight in the range 0.0 to 1.0. At normal incidence (head-on view)
   the output reaches its minimum; at grazing angles it reaches 1.0 (maximum reflection).
   For a typical IOR of 1.5, the minimum value at normal incidence is approximately 0.04,
   corresponding to the ~4% reflection that even glass has when viewed straight-on.
   Use this as the *Fac* input of a *Mix Shader* node to blend between two shaders.
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/input/fresnel.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Fresnel Node > Glass Material (Refraction + Reflection)
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes > Input Fresnel Node Glass Material (Refraction + Reflection)
text:
A classic glass setup using the Fresnel node:

- Connect the *Fresnel* node's *Factor* to the *Fac* of a *Mix Shader* node.
- Connect a *Glossy BSDF* (with roughness near 0.0) to the first shader input (refraction).
- Connect a second *Glossy BSDF* (also low roughness) to the second shader input (reflection).
- Set *IOR* to 1.5 for typical glass. At grazing angles, the reflection dominates;
  looking straight through, the refraction shows.
- Note: in modern Blender, a *Glass BSDF* or *Principled BSDF* with *Transmission*
  handles glass more conveniently. This manual setup is shown to illustrate
  how Fresnel-driven mixing works and can be applied to custom effects.
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/input/fresnel.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Fresnel Node > Plastic with Glossy Coating
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes > Input Fresnel Node Plastic with Glossy Coating
text:
Create plastic or clear-coated materials by mixing a diffuse base with a glossy top layer:

- Connect the *Factor* output to the *Fac* of a *Mix Shader* node.
- Connect a *Diffuse BSDF* to the first shader input (the base material).
- Connect a *Glossy BSDF* to the second shader input (the coating).
- Set *IOR* to 1.5 for standard plastic. At edges, the glossy coating reflects the environment;
  straight-on, the diffuse color shows through.
- Adjust the *Glossy BSDF* roughness to control the sharpness of reflections.
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/input/fresnel.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Fresnel Node > Environment Map Reflection
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes > Input Fresnel Node Environment Map Reflection
text:
Use the Fresnel weight to control the strength of an environment map:

- Connect the *Factor* output to the *Fac* of a *Mix Shader* node.
- Connect a *Diffuse BSDF* to the first shader input.
- Connect a *Glossy BSDF* (with low roughness) to the second shader input,
  with an *Environment Texture* driving its color.
- For a simple non-physical glow, an *Emission* shader can also be used.
- Lower the *IOR* (e.g. 0.9) to widen the reflective band and make the
  environment map more prominent across the surface.
- At edges, the environment is strongly visible, simulating a reflective coating.
- This creates a non-destructive way to add edge reflections without altering
  the base material.
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/input/fresnel.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Geometry Node
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes > Input Geometry Node Geometry Node
text:
The *Geometry* node gives geometric information about the current shading point.
All vector coordinates are in *World Space*. For volume shaders,
only the position and incoming vector are available.
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/input/geometry.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Geometry Node > Outputs
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes > Input Geometry Node Outputs
text:
Position
   Position of the shading point.
Normal
   Shading normal at the surface (includes smooth normals and bump mapping).
Tangent
   Tangent at the surface.
True Normal
   Geometry or flat normal of the surface.
Incoming
   Vector pointing towards the point the shading point is being viewed from.
Parametric
   Parametric coordinates of the shading point on the surface.
   To area lights it outputs its UV coordinates in planar mapping and
   in spherical coordinates to point lights.
Backfacing
   1.0 if the face is being viewed from the back side, 0.0 for the front side.
Pointiness Cycles Only
   An approximation of the curvature of the mesh per vertex.
   Lighter values indicate convex angles, darker values indicate concave angles.
   It allows you to do effects like dirt maps and wear-off effects.
Random per Island Cycles Only
   A random value for each connected component (island) of the mesh.
   It is useful to add variations to meshes composed of separated units
   like tree leaves, wood planks, or curves of multiple splines.
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/input/geometry.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Curves Info Node > Outputs
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes > Input Curves Info Node Outputs
text:
Is Strand
   Outputs 1 when the shader is acting on a strand, otherwise 0.
Intercept
   The point along the strand where the ray hits the strand (1 at the tip and 0 at the root).
Length
   The total measurement from the root to the tip of the strand,
   interpreted as a grayscale value from 0 to infinity.
Thickness
   The thickness of the strand at the point where the ray hits the strand.
Tangent Normal
   Tangent normal of the strand.
Random
   A random per-curve value in the range from 0 to 1.
   It can for example be used in combination with a color ramp, to randomize the curve's color.
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/input/hair_info.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Layer Weight Node
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes > Input Layer Weight Node Layer Weight Node
text:
The *Layer Weight* node outputs weight values used for blending between two shaders
via the *Mix Shader* node. It provides two types of angle-dependent weights that control
how much of each shader is visible at different viewing angles.

It is most commonly used to create realistic materials where the surface appearance
changes depending on whether you are looking at it head-on or at a glancing angle —
such as a glossy coating over a rough base, or edge highlights on a diffuse surface.
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/input/layer_weight.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Layer Weight Node > Inputs
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes > Input Layer Weight Node Inputs
text:
Blend
   Controls the spread and sharpness of the transition. The default value of
   0.5 is a good starting point. Higher values sharpen the edge, lower values
   produce a wider, more gradual blend.
   For the *Fresnel* output, *Blend* maps to the index of refraction:
   0.5 corresponds to IOR 1.5 (glass/plastic), lower values approximate lower
   IOR (weaker reflection), higher values produce stronger, mirror-like reflection.
Normal
   Optional input for a bump or normal map. When connected, the surface angle
   at each point is modified by the bump/normal detail before computing the weight.
   This makes the weight respond to surface texture — raised areas and depressions
   produce different blending values, adding realism to layered materials.
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/input/layer_weight.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Layer Weight Node > Outputs
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes > Input Layer Weight Node Outputs
text:
Fresnel
   Dielectric Fresnel weight in the range 0.0 to 1.0. At 0.0 the surface is
   viewed head-on (no Fresnel effect); at 1.0 the surface is at a grazing angle
   (maximum reflection). Use this as the *Fac* input of a *Mix Shader* node.

   Common use: mix a diffuse base shader with a glossy coating shader
   to create plastic or clear-coated materials.

Facing
   Geometric angle weight in the range 0.0 to 1.0. Outputs 1.0 when the surface
   directly faces the viewer, and 0.0 when viewed at a grazing angle.
   Unlike *Fresnel*, this output is not affected by the index of refraction —
   it is purely based on surface orientation.

   Common use: create edge glow or rim light effects by placing an *Emission*
   shader in the first slot of a *Mix Shader* node (since Fac = 0 at edges
   shows the first shader), with a diffuse surface in the second slot.

Tip:

   Use *Fresnel* when you need physically accurate reflection (plastic, glass, coated).
   Use *Facing* for artistic control or when IOR-based behavior is not desired.
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/input/layer_weight.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Layer Weight Node > Glossy Coating over Diffuse (Fresnel)
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes > Input Layer Weight Node Glossy Coating over Diffuse (Fresnel)
text:
A classic setup for plastic or clear-coated materials:

- Connect the *Fresnel* output to the *Fac* input of a *Mix Shader* node.
- Connect a *Diffuse BSDF* to the first shader input (the base).
- Connect a *Glossy BSDF* to the second shader input (the coating).
- Adjust *Blend* to control how strong the reflection appears at edges.
- At grazing angles, the glossy coating dominates; straight-on, the diffuse base shows through.
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/input/layer_weight.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Layer Weight Node > Edge Glow with Emission (Facing)
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes > Input Layer Weight Node Edge Glow with Emission (Facing)
text:
Since *Facing* outputs 1.0 at the center and 0.0 at edges,
place the emission in the first shader slot of the *Mix Shader* node:

- Connect the *Facing* output to the *Fac* input of a *Mix Shader* node.
- Connect an *Emission* shader to the first shader input.
- Connect a *Diffuse BSDF* (or *Principled BSDF*) to the second shader input.
- At the center (Fac ≈ 1.0), the second shader (diffuse) dominates.
- At the edges (Fac ≈ 0.0), the first shader (emission) dominates,
  creating a rim light effect.

Alternatively, use the *Fresnel* output for a more intuitive setup:
connect *Diffuse* to the first slot, *Emission* to the second slot —
*Fresnel* naturally puts the weight at the edges.
Adjust *Blend* to control the width of the glow band.
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/input/layer_weight.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Layer Weight Node > Bump/Normal Map Interaction
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes > Input Layer Weight Node Bump/Normal Map Interaction
text:
To make the weight respond to surface texture:

- Connect a *Noise Texture* to a *Bump* node.
- Connect the *Bump* node output to the *Normal* input of the *Layer Weight* node.
- Now the *Fresnel* (or *Facing*) weight varies across the bumps —
  raised areas and depressions produce different mixing values,
  giving the material surface a more realistic, detailed appearance.
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/input/layer_weight.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Light Evaluation Node
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes > Input Light Evaluation Node Light Evaluation Node
text:
EEVEE Only

The *Light Evaluation* node computes shading reflection factors, direction, distance,
and attenuation masks for the light source currently being evaluated.

Note:

   This node must be used alongside Light Accumulation.
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/input/light_evaluation.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Light Evaluation Node > Inputs
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes > Input Light Evaluation Node Inputs
text:
Position
   Evaluation position. Defaults to the shading surface position.
Normal
   Evaluation normal. Defaults to the geometry shading normal.
Roughness
   Surface roughness value. Used to compute the *Factor* output when *Mode* is set to *Glossy*.
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/input/light_evaluation.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Light Evaluation Node > Properties
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes > Input Light Evaluation Node Properties
text:
Mode
   Selects the shading model used to compute the *Factor* output (e.g. *Diffuse* or *Glossy*).
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/input/light_evaluation.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Light Evaluation Node > Outputs
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes > Input Light Evaluation Node Outputs
text:
Factor
   Calculated shading reflection factor (diffuse or glossy depending on *Mode*), scaled by PI.

Mask
   | *Point & Area lights:* Smooth cutoff mask applied at the light boundary distance.
   | *Spot lights:* Cutoff mask combined with spot cone angular attenuation.
   | *Sun lights:* 1.0 (sun lights do not attenuate by distance or cone angle).

Direction
   | *Point, Spot & Area lights:* Normalized unit vector pointing from the evaluation position toward the light position.
   | *Sun lights:* Reverse direction vector of the sun light rays (Sun direction * -1.0).

Distance
   | *Point, Spot & Area lights:* Distance from the evaluation position to the light position.
   | *Sun lights:* 1.0.
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/input/light_evaluation.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Light Info Node
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes > Input Light Info Node Light Info Node
text:
EEVEE Only

The *Light Info* node outputs basic properties (color, power,
and position) of the light source currently being evaluated.

Note:
   This node must be used alongside Light Accumulation.
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/input/light_info.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Light Info Node > Outputs
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes > Input Light Info Node Outputs
text:
Color
   The color of the evaluated light source, matching the *Color* setting in Properties > Light.
Power
   The radiant intensity of the evaluated light source, divided by PI.
Position
   The world-space position of the evaluated light source.
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/input/light_info.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Light Path Node
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes > Input Light Path Node Light Path Node
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/input/light_path.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Light Path Node > Outputs
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes > Input Light Path Node Outputs
text:
Is Camera Ray
   1.0 if shading is executed for a camera ray, otherwise 0.0.
Is Shadow Ray
   1.0 if shading is executed for a shadow ray, otherwise 0.0.
Is Diffuse Ray
   1.0 if shading is executed for a diffuse ray, otherwise 0.0.
Is Glossy Ray
   1.0 if shading is executed for a glossy ray, otherwise 0.0.
Is Singular Ray Cycles Only
   1.0 if shading is executed for a singular ray, otherwise 0.0.
Is Reflection Ray Cycles Only
   1.0 if shading is executed for a reflection ray, otherwise 0.0.
Is Transmission Ray Cycles Only
   1.0 if shading is executed for a transmission ray, otherwise 0.0.
Is Volume Scatter Ray Cycles Only
   1.0 if shading is executed for a volume scatter ray, otherwise 0.0.
Ray Length Cycles Only
   Distance traveled by the light ray from the last bounce or camera.
Ray Depth
   Number of times the ray has been reflected or transmitted on interaction with a surface.

Note:

      Passing through a
      transparent
      shader does not count as a normal "bounce".

Diffuse Depth Cycles Only
   Number of times the ray has gone through diffuse reflection or transmission.
Glossy Depth Cycles Only
   Number of times the ray has gone through glossy reflection or transmission.
Transparent Depth Cycles Only
   Number of times the ray has gone through a transparent surface.
Transmission Depth Cycles Only
   Number of times the ray has gone through a transmissive surface.
   A typical use case is to avoid black spots in the render (caused by rays hitting
   the bounce limit) by switching from a transmissive to a diffuse shader past a
   certain point. See mix.
Portal Depth: Cycles Only
   Number of times the ray has passed through a ray portal.
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/input/light_path.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Light Path Node > EEVEE Support
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes > Input Light Path Node EEVEE Support
text:
EEVEE has no real concept of rays, but in order to ease the workflow between Cycles and EEVEE,
some of the outputs are supported in particular cases.

- *Is Camera*: Supported.
- *Is Shadow*: Supported.
- *Is Diffuse*: Supported.
- *Is Glossy*: Supported.
- *Is Singular*: Not supported. Same as *Is Glossy*.
- *Is Reflection*: Not supported. Same as *Is Glossy*.
- *Is Transmission*: Not supported. Same as *Is Glossy*.
- *Ray Length*: Distance from the camera to the shading point.
- *Ray Depth*: Indicates the current bounce when baking the light cache.
- *Diffuse Depth*: Same as Ray Depth but only when baking diffuse light.
- *Glossy Depth*: Same as Ray Depth but only when baking specular light.
- *Transparent Depth*: Not supported. Defaults to 0.
- *Transmission Depth*: Not supported. Same as *Glossy Depth*.

Note:

   *Is Glossy* does not work with Screen Space Reflections/Refractions
   but does work with reflection planes (whether used with SSR or not).
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/input/light_path.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Particle Info Node
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes > Input Particle Info Node Particle Info Node
text:
Cycles Only

The *Particle Info* node can be used in the material node tree for objects that are used as the instancing objects,
when you use *Object* or *Collection* Render mode of a particle system.

This node gives access to the data of the particle that spawned the object instance.
It can be useful to give some variation to a single material assigned to multiple instances of instancing object.

Note:

   This node currently only supports parent particles. Info from child particles is not available.
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/input/particle_info.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Particle Info Node > Outputs
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes > Input Particle Info Node Outputs
text:
Index
   Index number of the particle (from 0 to number of particles).
Random
   A random per-particle value in the range from 0 to 1.
   It can for example be used in combination with a color ramp, to randomize the particle color.
Age
   Age of the particle in frames.
Lifetime
   Total lifespan of the particle in frames.
Location
   Location of the particle.
Size
   Size of the particle.
Velocity
   Velocity of the particle.
Angular Velocity
   Angular velocity of the particle.
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/input/particle_info.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Point Info
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes > Input Point Info Point Info
text:
Cycles Only

The *Point Info* node can be used in the material node tree for point cloud objects
and gives access to the data of individual points.
It can be useful to give some variation to a single material assigned a point cloud object.
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/input/point_info.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Point Info > Outputs
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes > Input Point Info Outputs
text:
Location
   Location of the particle.
Radius
   Size of the particle.
Random
   A random per-point value in the range from 0 to 1.
   It can for example be used in combination with a color ramp, to randomize the point color.
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/input/point_info.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Raycast Node > Attributes
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes > Input Raycast Node Attributes
text:
Cycles Only

Geometry attributes at the intersection point can be accessed.
Add attributes in the Sample Attributes panel in the node editor sidebar,
and new attribute sockets appear on the node.
Fill in the attribute name and link the new output socket to use the value.
When no intersection is found, the attribute output is zero.

EEVEE does not support attribute access, and outputs attributes as zero.
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/input/raycast.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Shadow Raycast Node
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes > Input Shadow Raycast Node Shadow Raycast Node
text:
EEVEE Only

The *Shadow Raycast* node provides a shadow mask for the light source currently being evaluated.

Note:

   This node must be used alongside Light Accumulation.
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/input/shadow_raycast.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Shadow Raycast Node > Inputs
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes > Input Shadow Raycast Node Inputs
text:
Position
   Evaluation position. Defaults to the shading surface position.
   If a custom position offsets the evaluation point beyond the object's bounding box,
   the material's Max Distance setting must be
   increased accordingly to prevent missing shadows artifacts.
Softness
   Shadow softness scaling factor. A value of 0.0 forces sharp shadows regardless of the light size,
   while 1.0 matches the physically correct shadow penumbra size.
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/input/shadow_raycast.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Shadow Raycast Node > Outputs
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes > Input Shadow Raycast Node Outputs
text:
Color
   The calculated shadow mask (a grayscale color value where 1.0 represents unoccluded light and 0.0
   represents fully occluded shadow).
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/input/shadow_raycast.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Tangent Node > Properties
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes > Input Tangent Node Properties
text:
Direction Type
   The tangent direction can be derived from a cylindrical projection around the X,
   Y, or Z axis (radial), or from a manually created UV Map for full control.
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/input/tangent.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Texture Coordinate Node
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes > Input Texture Coordinate Node Texture Coordinate Node
text:
The *Texture Coordinate* node outputs various coordinate systems
that can be used for procedural textures, image textures, and other vector-based texture inputs.

It is most commonly connected to the *Vector* input of texture nodes,
allowing textures to be placed or manipulated in different coordinate spaces.
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/input/texture_coordinate.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Texture Coordinate Node > Properties
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes > Input Texture Coordinate Node Properties
text:
Object
   Specific object to use for object space coordinates.
   This only affects the *Object* output.

From Instancer Cycles Only
   If the object is generated by instancing from vertices or faces, use texture coordinates from instancer.
   This only affects the *Generated* and *UV* outputs.

Note:

      *From Instancer* only works with the UV output when the object is instanced,
      either from particles or
      from faces.
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/input/texture_coordinate.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Texture Coordinate Node > Outputs
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes > Input Texture Coordinate Node Outputs
text:
Generated
   Automatically-generated texture coordinates from the vertex positions of the mesh without deformation,
   keeping them sticking to the surface under animation.
   Range from 0.0 to 1.0 over the bounding box of the non-deformed mesh.
   See Texture Spaces for more information.
Normal
   Object space normal, for texturing objects with the texture staying fixed on the object as it transformed.
   The Normal output can be used on Point and Spot lights. The coordinates will take
   the rotation of the light into account.
UV
   UV texture coordinates from the Active Render UV map.
   See UV Mapping for more information.

Note:

      To use a UV map other than the active one, use the
      UV Map node.
Object
   Uses an object as a source for coordinates. Often used with an empty,
   this is an easy way to place a small image at a given point on the object.
   This object can also be animated, to move a texture around or through a surface.
Camera
   Position coordinate in camera space.
Window
   Location of shading point on the screen, ranging from 0.0 to 1.0
   from the left to right side and bottom to top of the render.
   This is well suited for blending two objects.
Reflection
   Uses the direction of the reflection vector as coordinates.
   This is useful for adding reflection maps. You will need this input when using environment maps.
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/input/texture_coordinate.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: UV Map Node
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes > Input UV Map Node UV Map Node
text:
The *UV Map* node outputs texture coordinates from a specific UV map.
It is especially useful when working with multiple UV layouts in the same material.
The node is most commonly connected to the *Vector* input of texture nodes,
allowing textures to be placed or manipulated.

Note:

   Unlike the Texture Coordinate Node,
   which only outputs the active render UV map, this node can access any UV map assigned to the object.
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/input/uv_map.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: UV Map Node > Properties
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes > Input UV Map Node Properties
text:
From Instancer Cycles Only
   See the From Instancer
   option of the Texture Coordinate Node.

UV Map
   The name of the UV map to use.
   This list is populated from the UV maps available on the object's mesh data-block.
   If left unset, the Active Render UV map is used.
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/input/uv_map.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Color Attribute Node
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes > Input Color Attribute Node Color Attribute Node
text: The *Color Attribute* node provides access to Color Attributes as well as their alpha value.
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/input/vertex_color.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Color Attribute Node > Properties
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes > Input Color Attribute Node Properties
text:
Color Attribute
   The target Color Attribute.
   The listed Color Attributes are those of the mesh of the active object.
   If the active object has no mesh, a warning will be displayed.
   If the property is marked in red, it means the Color Attribute is not available in
   the mesh of the active object, but it may be available in other meshes of
   objects that share this material!
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/input/vertex_color.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Volume Info Node > Outputs
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes > Input Volume Info Node Outputs
text:
Color
   Gives the color of the smoke inside the Fluid Domain.
   The color and vector outputs are the same. The Factor output is an average of the channels.
Density
   Gives a scalar defining the density of any smoke inside
   the Fluid Domain.
Flame
   Gives a scalar defining the density of any fire inside
   the Fluid Domain.
   All three outputs are the same.
Temperature
   Gives a scalar defining the temperature of the volume. Values in the range 0 - 1 map to 0 - 1000 kelvin.
   This may be used to render physically-based fire with the Blackbody or Principled Volume shaders.
   All three outputs are the same.
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/input/volume_info.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Wireframe Node
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes > Input Wireframe Node Wireframe Node
text:
The Wireframe node is used to retrieve the edges of an object as it appears to Cycles.
As meshes are triangulated before being processed by Cycles,
topology will always appear triangulated when viewed with the Wireframe node.
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/input/wireframe.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Wireframe Node > Properties
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes > Input Wireframe Node Properties
text:
Pixel Size
   When enabled, the size of edge lines is set in screen space.
Size
   Thickness of the edge lines.
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/input/wireframe.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Wireframe Node > Outputs
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes > Input Wireframe Node Outputs
text:
Factor
   Black-and-white mask showing white lines representing edges according to the object's Topology.
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/input/wireframe.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Introduction > Shaders
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes Introduction Shaders
text:
An important concept to understand when building node setups is
that of the *shader socket*. The output of all surface and
volume shaders is a shader, describing lighting interaction at the surface or of the volume,
rather than the color of the surface.

There are a few types of shaders available as nodes:

BSDF (Bidirectional Scattering Distribution Function) shader
   Describe light reflection, refraction and absorption at an object surface.
Emission shader
   Describe light emission at an object surface or in a volume.
Volume shader
   Describe light scattering inside a volume.
Background shader
   Describe light emission from the environment.

Each shader node has a color input, and outputs a shader.
These can then be mixed and added together using Mix and Add Shader nodes.
No other operations are permitted.
The resulting output can then be used by the renderer to compute all light interactions,
for direct lighting or global illumination.

Seealso:

   Shaders
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/introduction.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Introduction > Textures
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes Introduction Textures
text:
Blender has various built in procedural texture nodes,
with texture coordinates and various parameters as input, and a color or value as output.
No texture data-blocks are needed; instead node groups can be used for reusing texture setups.

For UV mapping and texture painting in the 3D Viewport, the Image Texture node must be used.
When setting such a node as active, it will be displayed in the 3D Viewport
while using Texture color mode.
This method can be used to preview painted textures while texture painting.

The default texture coordinates for all nodes are Generated coordinates,
except for Image textures that use UV coordinates by default.
Each node includes some options to modify the texture mapping and resulting color,
and these can be edited in the texture properties.

Seealso:

   Textures
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/introduction.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Introduction > More
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes Introduction More
text:
Nodes for geometric data, texture coordinates,
layering shaders and non-physically-based tricks can be found in:

- Vector Nodes
- Color Nodes
- Utilities Nodes
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/introduction.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: AOV Output Node
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes > Output AOV Output Node AOV Output Node
text:
Shader AOVs (Arbitrary Output Variables) provide custom render passes for arbitrary shader node components.
As an artist this can be a good way to debug or tweak very fine details of a scene in post-processing.
To use shader AOVs create the pass in the Shader AOV panel
then reference that pass with the *AOV Output* shading node.
Shader AOVs can be added or removed in the *Shader AOV* panel.

Tip:

   The *AOV Output* node can be used in Material and World shader nodes.
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/output/aov.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: AOV Output Node > Inputs
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes > Output AOV Output Node Inputs
text:
Color
   Output a color variable; as the name suggest can be used for a color but also a normal value.
Value
   Output a single numerical value.
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/output/aov.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: AOV Output Node > Properties
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes > Output AOV Output Node Properties
text:
Name
   The name of the render pass to assign the input value to.
   This property has the same *Name* that is specified in the Shader AOV panel.
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/output/aov.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Output Nodes
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes > Output Output Nodes Output Nodes
text:
Output nodes are the final node in every node tree.
Although you can add more than one, only one will be used (indicated by a colored or darkened header).
Output nodes are always preceded by Shaders
except in the case of the Displacement of a Material Output.
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/output/index.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Light Output Node
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes > Output Light Output Node Light Output Node
text:
The *Light Output* node defines the final shader used by a
Light object.

It is used to control how a light emits energy in the scene using shader nodes.
Currently, light shaders are only supported by the Cycles render engine.
When evaluated in other contexts or renderers, the node has no effect.

See cycles-light-nodes for more information about using shader nodes with lights.
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/output/light.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Light Output Node > Inputs
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes > Output Light Output Node Inputs
text:
Surface
   Shader defining the emitted light.
   Typically this is an Emission shader,
   which controls the light's color and intensity.
   Only emission-based shading affects lighting; other shader types have no effect
   when connected to a light.
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/output/light.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Light Output Node > Properties
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes > Output Light Output Node Properties
text:
Target
   Specifies which render engine the connected shader applies to.

   :All: The shader is used by all render engines.
   :Cycles: The shader is only used when rendering with Cycles.
   :EEVEE: The shader is only used when rendering with EEVEE.

   Using multiple *Light Output* nodes with different targets allows creating
   renderer-specific light setups.
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/output/light.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Material Output Node
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes > Output Material Output Node Material Output Node
text: The *Material Output* node is used to output surface material information to a surface object.
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/output/material.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Material Output Node > Inputs
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes > Output Material Output Node Inputs
text:
Surface
   Shading for the surface of the object.
Volume
   Shading for the volume inside the object.
Displacement
   Used to create bump mapping or actual subdivided displacement.
Thickness EEVEE
   Used to approximate the inner geometry structure of the object without heavy computation.
   This is currently used for Subsurface Scattering,
   Translucent BSDF,
   Refraction BSDF, and the nodes containing these effects.

   If no value is plugged into the output node,
   a default thickness based on the smallest dimension of the object is used.
   If a value is connected it will be used as object space thickness (i.e. scaled by object transform).
   A value of zero will disable the thickness approximation and treat the object as having only one interface.

   This output is only used by the EEVEE render engine.

Note:

      - The thickness is used to skip the inner part of the object.
      - Refraction will not refract objects inside the thickness distance.
      - Shadow casting object will not cast shadow within the thickness distance.

Tip:

      - For large or compound meshes (e.g. vegetation),
        the thickness should be set to the thickness of individual parts (e.g. leaves, grass blades).
      - Thickness can be baked to textures or custom attributes for more accurate result.

Seealso:

      Thickness Mode -- controls how the thickness value is used.
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/output/material.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Material Output Node > Properties
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes > Output Material Output Node Properties
text:
Target
   Render engine the input shaders are used for.
   By default shaders are shared between Cycles and EEVEE,
   with multiple output nodes specialized shader setups can be created for each.
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/output/material.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: World Output Node
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes > Output World Output Node World Output Node
text:
The *World Output* node is used to output color information to the scene's
World.

To access this node, change the *Shader Type* in the header of
the Shader Editor to *World*.
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/output/world.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: World Output Node > Inputs
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes > Output World Output Node Inputs
text:
Surface
   The appearance of the environment.
   Usually connected to a Background shader.
Volume
   Used to add volumetric effects to the world.
   See the shaders Principled Volume,
   Volume Absorption,
   and Volume Scatter for more information.

Note:

      It's not possible to have a Surface and a Volume at the same time: surfaces are assumed to be
      at an infinite distance from the camera, so they will always be fully occluded by the volume.
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/output/world.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: World Output Node > Properties
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes > Output World Output Node Properties
text:
Target
   Render engine the input shaders are used for.
   By default, shaders are shared between Cycles and EEVEE --
   with multiple output nodes, a specialized shader setup can be created for each.

name: Diffuse BSDF

The *Diffuse* BSDF (Bidirectional Scattering Distribution Function)
node is used to add Lambertian and Oren-Nayar diffuse reflection.

name: Emission > Inputs

Color

Strength

name: Glass BSDF
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes > Shader Glass BSDF Glass BSDF
text:
The *Glass* BSDF (Bidirectional Scattering Distribution Function)
is used to add a Glass-like shader mixing refraction and reflection at grazing angles.
Like the transparent shader, only pure white will make it transparent.
The glass shader tends to cause noise due to caustics.
Since the Cycles path tracing integrator is not very good at rendering caustics,
it helps to combine this with a transparent shader for shadows;
for more details see here.
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/shader/glass.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Glass BSDF > Inputs
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes > Shader Glass BSDF Inputs
text:
Color
   Color of the surface, or physically speaking, the probability that light is transmitted for each wavelength.
Roughness
   Influences sharpness of the refraction; perfectly sharp at 0.0 and smoother with higher values.
Anisotropy Cycles Only
   Controls the amount the reflection and refraction stretch along the surface of the material.
   A value of 0.0 means isotropic.
   Higher values give elongated highlights orthogonal to the tangent direction;
   negative values give highlights shaped along the tangent direction.
Rotation Cycles Only
   Rotation of the anisotropic tangent direction.
   Value 0.0 equals 0° rotation, 0.25 equals 90° and 1.0 equals 360° = 0°.
   This can be used to texture the tangent direction.
IOR
   Index of refraction (IOR) defining how much the ray changes direction. At 1.0
   rays pass straight through like transparent; higher values give more refraction.
Normal
   Normal used for shading; if nothing is connected the default shading normal is used.
Tangent
   Tangent used for shading; if nothing is connected the default shading tangent is used.
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/shader/glass.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Glass BSDF > Thin Film :guilabel:`Cycles Only`
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes > Shader Glass BSDF Thin Film :guilabel:`Cycles Only`
text:
Thin Film simulates the effect of interference in a thin film sitting on top of the material.
This causes the specular reflection to be colored in a way which strongly depends on the view
angle as well as the film thickness and the index of refraction (IOR) of the film and
the material itself.

This effect is commonly seen on e.g. oil films, soap bubbles or glass coatings. While its
influence is more obvious in specular highlights, it also affects transmission.

Thickness
   The thickness of the film in nanometers. A value of 0 disables the simulation.
   The interference effect is strongest between roughly 100 and 1000 nanometers, since this is
   near the wavelengths of visible light.
IOR
   Index of refraction (IOR) of the thin film.
   The common range for this value is between 1.0 (vacuum and air) and roughly 2.0,
   though some materials can reach higher values.
   The default value of 1.33 is a good approximation for water.
   Note that when the value is set to 1.0 or to the main IOR of the material, the thin film
   effect disappears since the film optically blends into the air or the material.
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/shader/glass.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Glass BSDF > Properties
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes > Shader Glass BSDF Properties
text:
Distribution
   Microfacet distribution to use.

   :GGX: GGX microfacet distribution.
   :Multiscatter GGX:
      Takes multiple scattering events between microfacets into account.
      This gives more energy conserving results, which would otherwise be visible as excessive darkening.
   :Beckmann: Cycles Only
      Beckmann microfacet distribution.
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/shader/glass.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Glossy BSDF
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes > Shader Glossy BSDF Glossy BSDF
text:
The *Glossy* BSDF (Bidirectional Scattering Distribution Function)
node is used to add reflection with microfacet distribution, used for materials such as metal or mirrors.
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/shader/glossy.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Glossy BSDF > Inputs
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes > Shader Glossy BSDF Inputs
text:
Color
   Color of the surface, or physically speaking, the probability that light is reflected for each wavelength.
Roughness
   Sharpness of the reflection; perfectly sharp at 0.0 and smoother with higher values.
Anisotropy Cycles Only
   Controls the amount the reflection stretches the reflection along the surface of the material.
   A value of 0.0 results in no anisotropic reflections.
   Higher values give elongated highlights orthogonal to the tangent direction;
   negative values give highlights shaped along the tangent direction.

   This is a phenomenon known as "Anisotropic Reflections" which is often seen in metallic materials.
Rotation
   Rotation of the anisotropic tangent direction.
   Value 0.0 equals 0° rotation, 0.25 equals 90° and 1.0 equals 360° = 0°.
   This can be used to texture the tangent direction.

Normal
   Normal used for shading; if nothing is connected the default shading normal is used.
Tangent
   Tangent used for shading; if nothing is connected the default shading tangent is used.
source: Blender Manual, https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/shader_nodes/shader/glossy.html, by the Blender Documentation Team, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Glossy BSDF > Properties
keywords: Render > Shader Nodes > Shader Glossy BSDF Properties
text:
Distribution
   Microfacet distribution to use.

   :GGX: GGX microfacet distribution.
   :Multiscatter GGX:
      Takes multiple scattering events between microfacets into account.
      This gives more energy conserving results, which would otherwise be visible as excessive darkening.
   :Beckmann: Cycles Only
