name: Gothic architecture > Angevin Gothic
keywords: architecture Gothic architecture Angevin Gothic
text:
The emergence of Plantagenet or Angevin Gothic occurred in what is now western France at the same time as that of Île-de-France. It was linked to the political context of the Anglo-French Plantagenet dynasty. Unlike Île-de-France Gothic, this architectural style is characterized by facades with a single portal. In most cases, the hall church pattern is followed, with aisles as high as the nave. Some major churches, like Angers Cathedral, even lack aisles entirely. On the walls, the vaulting shafts were reduced to thin engaged columns with little projection. Sometimes, as in the nave of Le Mans Cathedral or in the Church of Notre-Dame de la Couture of Le Mans, statues marked the springing of the vault ribs, subverting the structural logic of vaulting shafts.
It is above all the vaults that distinguish Angevin Gothic. Emerging in the mid-12th century, its vaulting system developed the domed forms used in the local Romanesque architecture (for example at Périgueux Cathedral). Angevin Gothic vaults had a similarly domical profile, with the central keystone rising high above the vault's perimeter to produce an undulating ridge, very different to vaults elsewhere in France. This emphatic division of bays was reinforced by the use of heavy rib profiles, as seen at Angers Cathedral. The more vertical vault thrusts meant that flying buttresses were unnecessary, with Poitiers Cathedral having a sheer east wall instead of a chevet. Addding ridge ribs to this form of vaulting created an octopartite vault. From the 13th century onwards, lighter and more numerous and ribs appear, including liernes, as in the Abbey of St Sergius, Angers. After the incorporation of the region into the kingdom of France, more standard French Gothic forms began to be introduced, such as the triple portal

name: Gothic architecture > Norman Gothic
keywords: architecture Gothic architecture Norman Gothic
text:
The Duchy of Normandy, which was ruled by the kings of England, quickly adopted the Gothic style. The first example in the region was the nave of Lisieux Cathedral (1167 or 1170–1174); its bishop, Arnulf of Lisieux, was close to Abbot Suger and attended the consecration of Saint-Denis in 1144. Early Gothic churches in Normandy were wide, with long transepts and heavy vaults requiring thick walls.
Following his victories over John of England, Philip Augustus annexed the territory to the French royal domain in 1204: the influence of Île-de-France Gothic art then rapidly appeared in military architecture. From Paris, the round tower of the medieval Louvre Castle inspired not only the keeps of Rouen and Lillebonne, but also the Talbot keeps of Falaise and Gisors.
The plan of Norman Gothic churches was distinguished by an enlarged chapel on the central axis of the chevet, which served as the lady chapel, as at Fécamp Abbey. The arches were characteristically very sharply pointed (also known as lancet arches) and deeply moulded, while the quadripartite vault was favoured over the sexpartite. Another distinctive feature of Norman Gothic, in common with English Gothic, was the use of a high lantern tower instead of a small flèche above the crossing. Such towers feature at almost all the region's cathedrals, including Lisieux, Coutances, Rouen and Évreux. Where they are absent, this may be due to the original plans being curtailed, as at Sées Cathedral.

Rouen Cathedral (begun 1185) was rebuilt from Romanesque to Gothic with distinct Norman features, including a lantern tower, deeply moulded decoration, and high pointed arcades. The choir of the abbey church of Saint-Étienne of Caen was the first major building constructed after the end of the duchy (1204). The choir follows the

name: Gothic architecture > Southern Gothic
keywords: architecture Gothic architecture Southern Gothic
text:
Southern Gothic, also known as Toulouse Gothic or Languedoc Gothic, developed in southern France following the victory of the French Crown and the Catholic Church over the Cathars in the Albigensian Crusade (1220-29). After the political eradication of the Cathar aristocracy, it remained necessary to reconquer people's minds. In addition to the establishment of the Inquisition, the reassertion of Catholic control led to the construction of many Gothic churches and other buildings. The Cathars had strongly opposed the luxury of the Roman Catholic Church, and an architectural style more austere and restrained than that of northern France was therefore favoured. This original style was conceived as a militant architecture, an important weapon of the Church in its struggle against Cathar dissent. Preaching was an important tool against Catharism, and for this reason the aisleless nave was favoured, for the congregation to see and hear the preacher better. However, the presence of a single nave is not necessarily connected with this intention, and may result from other considerations or from the prior existence of a single nave. These naves were flanked by side chapels instead of aisles, divided by internal buttress-walls.
Southern Gothic is characterised by an emphasis on massive, plain walls, frequently of brick. Internal buttresses were used instead of flying buttresses, which combined with narrow windows to create a monolithic exterior, as at Albi Cathedral.  This severe impression was reinforced by the lack of sculpture or moulding, which was difficult to achieve in brick. Pointed arches were also challenging to create, leading to the use of mitred (triangular-headed) arches as ornament. These arches were often applied to towers, which were generally octagonal in Tolous

name: Gothic architecture > Central Europe
keywords: architecture Gothic architecture Central Europe
text:
There was an initial distrust in German-speaking countries regarding the new style coming from France. Since the time of Charlemagne, and later under the Ottonians and the Hohenstaufen, master builders of the western regions of the Empire — and particularly in the Rhine basin between Basel and Cologne — had developed an original architectural style of strong Romanesque matrix. The transition was slow, and initially buildings fused Gothic characteristics with elements that were still typically Romanesque, like Magdeburg Cathedral (1208) and Limburg Cathedral (1211–35). Fully-Gothic buildings began to appear in Germany in the 1230s, such as the Elisabethkirche, Marburg (begun 1235 or 1236) and the Liebfrauenkirche, Trier (c. 1233–83).

Amiens Cathedral was the source of inspiration for Gerhard, the architect of Cologne Cathedral. Begun in 1248, its conception was extremely ambitious: the vaults rise above 43 metres. The choir was consecrated in 1322, but work progressed very slowly, only being completed in 1880, to the original designs.
The lengthy construction of Strasbourg Cathedral (which at the time was a city of the Empire) followed the artistic vicissitudes linked to the penetration of the Gothic style. The 12th century reconstruction initially followed late Romanesque lines, but the introduction of Parisian masons in the mid-13th century heralded a change to the Rayonnant style, of which the Strasbourg workshop soon became an important centre. The Rayonnant west front at Strasbourg exhibits harpstring tracery covering walls and windows alike, giving an intense verticality. This taste for tall and slender forms is also noticeable in Regensburg Cathedral (1285), and in the Sainte-Chapelle-inspired choir of Aachen Cathedral (begun in 1355).

name: Gothic architecture > Swabia and Bohemia
keywords: architecture Gothic architecture Swabia and Bohemia
text:
In Swabia and Bohemia, the late Gothic is linked to the Parler family of masons. The patriarch was Heinrich I the Elder, whose descendants extended their artistic influence across a large part of Bohemia, in the German-Austrian area, reaching as far as Brabant and Flanders. Their works are characterised by complex articulation of walls and vaults, but are not similar enough to be considered a distinct style.
Heinrich Parler and his son Peter both worked at the parish church of the Holy Cross in Schwäbisch-Gmünd (1320), in Swabia, reviving the model of the hall church based on the simplicity of the mendicant orders, but with innovative solutions in the choir (begun in 1350).

Peter Parler, in particular, was one of the great protagonists of the Late Gothic. In 1356, he was summoned to Prague by Emperor Charles IV to complete St. Vitus Cathedral, begun in 1344 by the French architect Mathieu d'Arras. Charles had made Prague the capital of the Empire and wanted to expand it with an ambitious plan, which included a Gothic palace, Karlstejn Castle, and buildings for the new University of Prague.
While working on St. Vitus, Parler broke the fluid rhythm of the ambulatory, added the monumental square-plan chapel dedicated to Saint Wenceslas, and crowned the interiors with a pioneering net vault, suggesting an awareness of English Decorated developments. Parler also worked on the construction of the All Saints' Chapel on the Hradčany hill (using the Sainte-Chapelle as a model), the famous Charles Bridge over the Vltava (1357), the choir of Kolín (1360), and the Frauenkirche in Nuremberg.
Peter Parler's family members were active throughout Europe: Wenzel was architect of the cathedral of Vienna (1400–1404), Johann IV worked on the choir of Kutná Hora, and Heinrich III was at th

name: Gothic architecture > Brick Gothic
keywords: architecture Gothic architecture Brick Gothic
text: In the northern Hanseatic and Baltic cities (such as Northern Germany and Poland), the lack of local stone led to the creation of a Gothic style based on brick, called Backsteingotik (Brick Gothic). The builders combined this less easily-worked material with the elevation and lightness of French Gothic, simplifying its forms without sacrificing ornamentation. The main examples of this style include St. Mary's Church in Lübeck (1250–1350), St. Mary's Church in Gdańsk (1379–1502), St. Mary's Basilica in Kraków (1290–1365), and Malbork Castle (13th century). The style was not limited only to religious architecture: entire urban plans were laid out according to the Gothic style of the Hanseatic regions, with the construction of civil and public buildings, such as the Holstentor gate in Lübeck, and structures in Chorin, Prenzlau, and Stralsund. In eastern Germany, Poland and the Baltic, the style is particularly associated with the Teutonic Knights.
source: Wikipedia, "Gothic architecture", https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gothic_architecture, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Gothic architecture > The Low Countries
keywords: architecture Gothic architecture The Low Countries
text:
In the Middle Ages, present-day Belgium and the Netherlands were part of the sphere of artistic influence of the Diocese of Cologne and France. However, it is in civil and public architecture that the Gothic style of this region reached its apogee. From the late 13th century onwards, the area of Flanders and Brabant was at the centre of a very rich commercial and textile network. The wealth of the bourgeoisie favoured the development of civic life, which manifested itself in grandiose buildings decorated in ashlar masonry: the hallen (large markets and merchandise warehouses) and town halls. To symbolise secular power, these civic buildings were endowed with towering belfries ('beffrois'), matching the scale of the great cathedrals. The Schepenhuis, Aalst (1225) was the typological reference point for town halls, with its corner turrets and continuous row of windows. The town halls of Bruges and Brussels present similar schemes, but with ornately decorated facades, a taste for late-Gothic detail also visible in the palaces of Mons (1458), Ghent (1518), Leuven (1448) and Oudenaarde (1526–1536).
Brabantine Gothic was characterised by the use of pale sandstone or limestone (which allowed for very meticulous carved details), columns with capitals of stylised foliage (such as cabbage leaves), and sometimes timber ceilings due to unstable soil conditions. Notable examples include the Church of Our Lady of the Sablon in Brussels (15th century), the Cathedral of St. Michael and St. Gudula (also in Brussels, begun in the 13th century), and the Grote Kerk, Haarlem, with its monumental wooden ceiling (c. 1479).
source: Wikipedia, "Gothic architecture", https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gothic_architecture, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Gothic architecture > Italy
keywords: architecture Gothic architecture Italy
text:
Notwithstanding the early Norman experiemnts with pointed arches in Sicily, the Gothic style arrived late in Italy and failed to take deep root due to the strong classical tradition present in the peninsula. Italian Gothic architecture was deeply influenced by the geopolitics of its city-states and the materials available in different regions: marble was available in large quantities in Tuscany, being generously used for surface cladding, while its scarcity in Lombardy induced the extensive use of brick. Many northern European architectural elements were rejected or profoundly subverted, reflecting architectural choices associated with Italian urban traditions and a detachment from the Île-de-France cathedral model. Thus, instead of dissolving the wall into an abstract structural system dominated by glass, Italian architecture preserved the mass and flatness of the wall, covering it with frescoes. The persistence of architectural solutions distinct from French cathedrals should not be understood as passive resistance or technical delay, but as an expression of Italian political and institutional structures. The monumental architecture of urban communes, the papacy, and the empire developed their own languages that hardly aligned with the model of centralised territorial monarchies of northern Europe.
The Cistercian monastic order played an important role in the initial diffusion of Burgundian Gothic in early 13th century Italy, as seen in Fossanova Abbey (consecrated in 1208) and Casamari Abbey (1203–1217). Although they followed the basic plan of Gothic Cistercian churches in Burgundy, particularly Cîteaux Abbey, the Cistercians also adopted local features.

name: Gothic architecture > Kingdom of Castile
keywords: architecture Gothic architecture Kingdom of Castile
text:
In the Iberian Peninsula, French Gothic elements were introduced by the Cistercians in the second half of the 12th century. The earliest examples were the monasteries of Veruela, Poblet, and Santes Creus. Ribbed vaults were very early applied inside buildings of still fully Romanesque matrix, such as the Portico of Glory of the Santiago de Compostela Cathedral or Zamora Cathedral. The Gothic style in the Iberian Peninsula differs from the rest of Europe, the result of a transitional period in which the end of the Romanesque alternated with rare expressions of pure Gothic. In 1172, the French architect Giral Fruchel designed the fortified Ávila Cathedral, which fuses Romanesque and Gothic forms. Inspired by the Basilica of Saint-Denis, King Alfonso VIII of Castile demanded for Ávila a plan with radiating chapels and a double ambulatory. The cathedral is notable for its early use of flying buttresses. 
In the 13th century, however, fundamental political changes had direct repercussions on Hispanic architecture. Muslims lost control of most of the peninsula: following the conquest of Seville in 1248, only the Kingdom of Granada remained under their domain. The kingdoms of Castile, Aragon, Portugal, and later Mallorca became the new Iberian powers. This was the time when the so-called Full Gothic (or High Gothic) arrived, and the cathedrals most closely linked to French and German Gothic - Toledo, Burgos and León - were erected. Spanish Gothic churches are comparatively wide and frequently feature very high arcades topped by low clerestories, giving them a spatiality similar to German hall churches. Some authors apply the qualifier "Gothic" with caution and favour the term "low medieval".

The reconstruction of Toledo Cathedral was begun in 1227 by Archbishop Rodrigo Jiméne

name: Gothic architecture > Catalonia, the Balearic Islands, and Valencia
keywords: architecture Gothic architecture Catalonia, the Balearic Islands, and Valencia
text:
Architectural development in this region is inseparable from its political, social, and territorial reality. The monarchy, consolidated from the time of Ramon Berenguer IV and the union with the Kingdom of Aragon, determined the guidelines of ecclesiastical architecture and allied with the urban bourgeoisie and merchant aristocracy, driving institutional and urban growth. Gothic architecture began to be introduced under James I (1213–1276), who expanded the territory by conquering Mallorca and Valencia. The late 13th century saw major civic projects, including the city wall, royal palace and drassanes (shipyards, 1281) in Barcelona, and the municipal palace of La Paeria in Lleida.

In the 14th century, several major churches were constructed in Barcelona, including the cathedral (begun in 1298), Santa Maria del Pi (begun c. 1320) and Santa Maria del Mar (1329-84). They shared an expansive mendicant-influenced spatiality, with very high arcades, small clerestory windows and internal wall buttresses between side-chapels. Girona Cathedral was begun along similar lines in 1312, but the design was changed in the 15th century to produce an even more unified space, with a single vault (the widest Gothic vault in the world) covering the width of both nave and aisles, supported by massive buttresses between the side chapels. The junction between the two sections is masked by three large rose windows.

On the island of Mallorca, Palma Cathedral is similarly ambitious, with a large nave supported by a complex hierarchy of buttresses. Construction began in the early 14th century, and its chevet was completed in 1327, though the cathedral was not finished until the 17th century. The choir lacks an ambulatory and is lower than the nave, which has a two-storey elevation with soaring f

name: Gothic architecture > Late Gothic in Spain
keywords: architecture Gothic architecture Late Gothic in Spain
text:
In contrast to other areas of Europe, cathedral building in Spain continued extensively into the later Middle Ages and beyond the end of the Gothic period, owing to the drawn-out Reconquista. The largest church of this period is Seville Cathedral (1401), designed with a five-aisled plan and chapels embedded directly into the exterior buttresses. The vaults rise to the level of the upper clerestory windows.
In 1469, the country achieved political unification as a result of the marriage between Ferdinand of Aragon and Isabella of Castile; in 1492, this was followed by the annexation of the Kingdom of Granada, until then the last Muslim domain, and in 1512 the Kingdom of Navarre was conquered, cementing Spain's place as a dominant European power. In the late 15th century, a new style called Isabelline thus spread, fusing the characteristics of Flamboyant Gothic with Mudéjar elements and early Renaissance influxes.
One example is the church of San Gil Abad in Burgos, where the Chapel of the Nativity of Mary (1529) uses squinches to convert the square plan into an octagonal one, crowned by a star vault with a central oculus, while the Chapel of the Three Kings (1489) is characterized by its geometric complexity and highly ornamented vault bosses, reflecting the direct influence of Burgos Cathedral.
Spanish Gothic from this phase resulted from close collaboration between local, German, Flemish, and French architects and artisans. Among the most prominent figures is Juan Guas, designer of the elaborate Franciscan San Juan de los Reyes in Toledo. The church, commissioned by the Catholic Monarchs, was intended to house the royal pantheon until the conquest of Granada (1492). Meanwhile Simón de Colonia designed the octagonal Constable's Chapel (1482–1494) in Burgos Cathedral, cro
source: Wikipedia, "Gothic architecture", https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gothic_architecture, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Gothic architecture > Portugal
keywords: architecture Gothic architecture Portugal
text:
In contrast to the scale and monumentality of northern European cathedrals, Portuguese Gothic is characterized by restrained volumes, conditioned by local materials. As in Spain, Gothic exteriors were frequently blocky and fortress-like, lacking spires or steep roofs. The first to introduce the style were the 12th century Cistercian monks, in the Alcobaça Monastery (1178-1252), the country's first entirely Gothic building. It has a chevet, rib vaults and flying buttresses. Simultaneously, military orders played a decisive role in spreading the new architecture, as in the Church of Santa Maria do Olival and the round church in the Convent of Christ, both in Tomar (Templars). Évora Cathedral and the cloister of the Old Cathedral of Coimbra also belong to this initial phase. The spread of Gothic architecture was enabled by contacts with the western French coastline and dynastic relations with the House of Évreux, introducing models that linked Portugal and the Asturias to southwestern France. However, the transition between Romanesque and Gothic proceeded slowly, throughout the 13th and 14th centuries. Conservative features like plate tracery were used as late as the 14th century, for example at the Monastery of Odivelas (1295–1305). Santarém was the centre of this transitional style. 
Cathedrals initiated in the Romanesque period, such as Porto and Lisbon, were completed or remodelled according to Gothic principles, frequently incorporating cloisters of Cistercian influence. Porto also has early flying buttresses. Only the Alcobaça Monastery, the Monastery of Santa Clara-a-Velha, Évora Cathedral, Guarda Cathedral and the Batalha Monastery are fully stone vaulted, with timber ceilings being more common in mendicant churches.
