name: Blender foundations (mesh anatomy, navigation and the shortcuts that make modeling fast) > Step 1: What a mesh is
keywords: art blender basics Blender foundations (mesh anatomy, navigation and the shortcuts that make modeling fast) Step 1: What a mesh is guide path tutorial
text:
**You'll learn:** A mesh is a list of **vertices** (points in space), **edges** (lines joining two vertices) and **faces** (flat surfaces filled in between 3 or more edges). Faces with 3 sides are triangles, 4 are **quads**, more are **n-gons**. The game engine only draws triangles, but quads are easier to work with because edge loops flow through them (Step 5). Each face has a **normal**: an arrow pointing out of its front side. Lighting uses normals, and faces seen from behind can turn invisible in games (back-face culling), so normals must point outward.
**Build:** Add a cube (Shift+A > Mesh > Cube). Press Tab for Edit Mode, then 1 (vertices), 2 (edges), 3 (faces). Open the Overlays menu (top right of the viewport) and turn on Face Orientation: blue is the front of a face, red is the back.
**Try it yourself:** Select one face (3, click it) and press Alt+N > Flip. It turns red. Press Shift+N (Recalculate Outside) to fix it. That's the fix for most "my model has holes in the game" problems.
**Done when:** You can say how many vertices, edges and faces a cube has (8, 12, 6) and what a red face means.
source: RusticEngine Blender Art Path 'art-blender-basics' step 1 (open it with game_path)

name: Blender foundations (mesh anatomy, navigation and the shortcuts that make modeling fast) > Step 2: Moving the view without thinking
keywords: art blender basics Blender foundations (mesh anatomy, navigation and the shortcuts that make modeling fast) Step 2: Moving the view without thinking guide path tutorial
text:
**Build:** Middle mouse drag orbits, Shift+middle drag pans, the wheel zooms. Numpad . frames the selection (Home frames everything). Numpad 1 front, 3 right, 7 top (Ctrl+ the same number for the opposite side), Numpad 5 switches perspective/orthographic. The ` key (left of 1) opens a view pie menu. No numpad? Edit > Preferences > Input > Emulate Numpad, or use the view gizmo in the top right.
**You'll learn:** Orthographic views have no perspective, so lengths and angles are true. Model the shape in ortho front/side/top, then check it in perspective.
**Try it yourself (drill):** Without the mouse: front (1), side (3), top (7), back (Ctrl+1), frame selected (Numpad .), toggle ortho (5). Do it three times in a row.
**Done when:** You never reach for the view gizmo.
source: RusticEngine Blender Art Path 'art-blender-basics' step 2 (open it with game_path)

name: Blender foundations (mesh anatomy, navigation and the shortcuts that make modeling fast) > Step 3: The transform keys G, R, S
keywords: art blender basics Blender foundations (mesh anatomy, navigation and the shortcuts that make modeling fast) Step 3: The transform keys G, R, S guide path tutorial
text:
**Build:** Select something and press G (grab/move), R (rotate) or S (scale). While moving, press X, Y or Z to lock to that axis (Shift+Z locks to everything except Z), type a number for an exact value (G Z 0.5 Enter), hold Ctrl to snap, Shift for fine control. Right click or Esc cancels. Pressing G twice on a vertex or edge slides it along the surface.
**You'll learn:** These three keys plus axis locks and numbers are about 40% of all modeling. Typed numbers make models clean and exact.
**Try it yourself (drill):** Make a box 2 m long, 0.5 m wide and 1 m tall from the default cube, using only S, X/Y/Z and typed numbers. Then press Ctrl+A > Scale. "Apply scale" bakes the size into the mesh. Bevels, modifiers and the game engine expect a scale of 1, so always apply scale before modeling details.
**Done when:** The N panel (press N) shows Dimensions 2 x 0.5 x 1 and Scale 1, 1, 1.
source: RusticEngine Blender Art Path 'art-blender-basics' step 3 (open it with game_path)

name: Blender foundations (mesh anatomy, navigation and the shortcuts that make modeling fast) > Step 4: Extrude, inset, bevel
keywords: art blender basics Blender foundations (mesh anatomy, navigation and the shortcuts that make modeling fast) Step 4: Extrude, inset, bevel guide path tutorial
text:
**Build:** In Edit Mode, face select (3): E extrudes (pulls the face out, building new side faces), I insets (shrinks a face inward, leaving a ring of faces), Ctrl+B bevels edges (rounds or chamfers them), and Ctrl+Shift+B bevels vertices. Scroll the mouse wheel during a bevel to add segments. After any tool, press F9 (or open the panel in the bottom left) to change its settings afterwards.
**You'll learn:** Almost any hard object is a box that has been extruded, inset and beveled. Bevels matter even on low-poly models: real objects never have perfectly sharp edges, and a small bevel catches light and makes the shape read.
**Try it yourself (drill):** Turn a cube into a simple crate: inset all six faces (select all with A, press I, then I again for individual faces), then extrude the insets inward (E, -0.05).
**Done when:** You can do the crate in under a minute, without menus.
source: RusticEngine Blender Art Path 'art-blender-basics' step 4 (open it with game_path)

name: Blender foundations (mesh anatomy, navigation and the shortcuts that make modeling fast) > Step 5: Edge loops and topology
keywords: art blender basics Blender foundations (mesh anatomy, navigation and the shortcuts that make modeling fast) Step 5: Edge loops and topology guide path tutorial
text:
**Build:** Ctrl+R adds a loop cut: hover over an edge, scroll to add more cuts, click, then slide or right-click to center. Alt+click an edge selects its whole loop; Ctrl+Alt+click selects a ring. K is the knife, J connects two selected vertices with an edge, M merges vertices, X deletes (and asks what), Ctrl+X dissolves without leaving a hole.
**You'll learn:** **Topology** is how the faces flow across the surface. Edge loops are rings of quads around a shape, like the lines of latitude on a globe. They decide where a model can bend (joints need loops), how it smooths (Subdivision Surface follows loops), and how easy it is to select and change. Triangles and n-gons stop loops, so keep them on flat areas where nothing bends.
**Try it yourself (drill):** Loop-cut a cylinder 4 times, select one loop (Alt+click) and scale it (S) to make a waist. Add Subdivision with Ctrl+2 in Object Mode and watch how the loops control the shape. Ctrl+0 removes it again.
**Done when:** You can explain why a joint needs extra loops.
source: RusticEngine Blender Art Path 'art-blender-basics' step 5 (open it with game_path)

name: Blender foundations (mesh anatomy, navigation and the shortcuts that make modeling fast) > Step 6: Modifiers (non-destructive modeling)
keywords: art blender basics Blender foundations (mesh anatomy, navigation and the shortcuts that make modeling fast) Step 6: Modifiers (non-destructive modeling) guide path tutorial
text:
**Build:** Properties > Modifiers (wrench) > Add Modifier. Mirror (model half, it copies the other side; turn on Clipping so the middle vertices stay joined), Bevel (rounds every edge without changing the mesh), Solidify (gives thickness to a flat surface), Array (repeats it), Subdivision Surface (Ctrl+1 to Ctrl+5 in Object Mode), Weighted Normal (makes beveled low-poly shading look clean). Ctrl+A > Apply when you're sure.
**You'll learn:** Modifiers are a stack of recipes applied on top of your mesh, top to bottom. Order matters: Mirror before Bevel bevels the joined result. The RusticEngine Link exports the result with every modifier applied, so you can keep them live in Blender.
**Done when:** You've built something with Mirror + Bevel + Weighted Normal and switched each one off and on to see what it does.
source: RusticEngine Blender Art Path 'art-blender-basics' step 6 (open it with game_path)

name: Blender foundations (mesh anatomy, navigation and the shortcuts that make modeling fast) > Step 7: Shading, smoothness and the look
keywords: art blender basics Blender foundations (mesh anatomy, navigation and the shortcuts that make modeling fast) Step 7: Shading, smoothness and the look guide path tutorial
text:
**Build:** Z opens the shading pie (Wireframe, Solid, Material Preview, Rendered). Alt+Z is X-ray (select through the model). Object > Shade Auto Smooth smooths curved faces but keeps sharp edges sharp (it adds a Smooth by Angle modifier).
**You'll learn:** Flat vs smooth shading only changes how normals are averaged, not the geometry. A "smooth" low-poly cylinder still has 16 sides; the lighting hides them. That's why normals also matter for baking later.
**Done when:** You can make a cylinder look round with only 12-16 sides.
source: RusticEngine Blender Art Path 'art-blender-basics' step 7 (open it with game_path)

name: Blender foundations (mesh anatomy, navigation and the shortcuts that make modeling fast) > Step 8: Get it into the game
keywords: art blender basics Blender foundations (mesh anatomy, navigation and the shortcuts that make modeling fast) Step 8: Get it into the game guide path tutorial
text:
**Build:** Open the RusticEngine tab in the sidebar (N), set your project once, press Export to RusticEngine, then tick Live Link. From now on Ctrl+S in Blender updates the game. Keep the .blend file outside the project folder.
**You'll learn:** 1 Blender unit = 1 meter = 1 unit in the engine. Apply scale (Ctrl+A) and put the origin where the object should stand (Object > Set Origin) before export.
**Done when:** Your crate is in your game, and changing it in Blender updates it there.

name: Blender foundations (mesh anatomy, navigation and the shortcuts that make modeling fast) > Step 9: Light it once, in Blender
keywords: art blender basics Blender foundations (mesh anatomy, navigation and the shortcuts that make modeling fast) Step 9: Light it once, in Blender guide path tutorial
text:
**Design question:** What time of day is your scene, and where does the light come from?
**Build:** Add a Sun (Shift+A > Light > Sun) and rotate it (R) until the shadows fall the way you want; Strength 3-5 is daylight. Add Point or Spot lights for lamps and torches (Watts in the Light properties), Area lights for windows. Set the world: World properties > Color for a plain sky, or an HDRI (Environment Texture, free CC0 skies on Poly Haven) for real outdoor light. Check it in Rendered view (Z > Rendered) with Cycles.
**You'll learn:** Light has units: a sun is measured per square meter (it's the same everywhere), a lamp in watts (it fades with the square of the distance: twice as far = a quarter as bright). RusticEngine rebuilds Blender's sun, point, spot and area lights with the same brightness, plus the world sky and your color management (AgX/Filmic and Exposure in Render properties > Color Management), when Send World is on in the RusticEngine panel. Area lights become soft spot lights (games have no true area lights). Turn Send World off for props, so only the level brings its sky.
**Try it yourself:** Move a point light twice as far from a wall and predict how much darker it gets before you look.
**Done when:** The scene looks the same in Blender's Rendered view and in your game.

name: buildings in Blender (a modular kit you can snap together) > Step 1: Style and grid
keywords: art blender building buildings in Blender (a modular kit you can snap together) Step 1: Style and grid guide path tutorial
text:
**Design question:** What era and culture? What does the player do in these buildings (enter them? only see them from outside?) That decides how much interior you need.
**You'll learn:** **The grid is everything.** Pick a module size and never break it: e.g. walls 2 m wide and 3 m tall, floors 2 x 2 m, door openings 1 x 2.2 m. Make the module fit your character: doors need room for the camera.
**Build:** Snapping: Shift+Tab toggles snapping, Ctrl+Shift+Tab chooses what to snap to (Increment, with "Absolute Grid Snap" on, so things land on the grid). Set the grid in the Overlays panel if you want 0.5 m steps.
**Done when:** You've written the module sizes down.

name: buildings in Blender (a modular kit you can snap together) > Step 2: The first wall piece
keywords: art blender building buildings in Blender (a modular kit you can snap together) Step 2: The first wall piece guide path tutorial
text:
**Build:** Add a plane, scale it to exactly 2 x 3 m with typed numbers (S X 2... or edit vertices with snapping), Solidify for thickness (0.2-0.3 m), apply scale (Ctrl+A). Put the origin on a bottom corner (Shift+S > Cursor to Selected on that vertex, Object > Set Origin > Origin to 3D Cursor).
**You'll learn:** Corner origins make pieces snap edge to edge in the engine with whole-number positions.
**Done when:** Two copies (Shift+D, X 2, Enter) meet with no gap and no overlap.

name: buildings in Blender (a modular kit you can snap together) > Step 3: The kit
keywords: art blender building buildings in Blender (a modular kit you can snap together) Step 3: The kit guide path tutorial
text:
**Build:** From the wall: wall with door (cut the opening with loop cuts Ctrl+R and delete faces, or a Boolean with a box: Bool Tool extension makes this quick), wall with window, corner piece (outer and inner), floor tile, stairs, roof slope and roof end. Keep all of them on the grid.
**You'll learn:** About 8-12 pieces build almost any building. Variation comes from combining them, not from more pieces.
**Done when:** You can build a small house from the kit in Blender by snapping alone.

name: buildings in Blender (a modular kit you can snap together) > Step 4: Shape and age
keywords: art blender building buildings in Blender (a modular kit you can snap together) Step 4: Shape and age guide path tutorial
text:
**Build:** Break perfect lines: move a few vertices on the roof ridge (G with proportional editing, O, scroll to change its radius), add timber beams (thin boxes) along the edges of the wall, bevel the stone corners. Keep the outer edges of each piece on the grid so pieces still fit.
**You'll learn:** **Proportional editing** moves nearby vertices with a falloff, which makes sagging roofs and bent beams in one move. Age is in the silhouette: a dead-straight roof looks like a toy.
**Done when:** It looks built by people, not by a computer.

name: buildings in Blender (a modular kit you can snap together) > Step 5: Trim sheets and tiling textures
keywords: art blender building buildings in Blender (a modular kit you can snap together) Step 5: Trim sheets and tiling textures guide path tutorial
text:
**Build:** Use tiling textures for big areas (stone, plaster, wood planks: free CC0 sets on Poly Haven and ambientCG) and a **trim sheet** for edges and beams. UVs: walls use a cube-like projection so stones are the same size everywhere; select faces and U > Cube Projection, or Smart UV Project. The free Texel Density Checker extension keeps scale consistent across pieces.
**You'll learn:** **Tiling** textures repeat seamlessly, so a 2 m wall and a 20 m wall use the same 1 texture with UVs that extend past 0-1. Matching texel density is what makes pieces look like one building.
**Done when:** Stones are the same size on every piece and no seams show where pieces meet.

**Build:** Barrel: cylinder (12-16 sides), Ctrl+R for 4 loops, scale the middle ones out (Alt+click, S), inset the top (I) and extrude it down (E) for the lid, select two loops and extrude along normals (Alt+E > Extrude Faces Along Normals) for metal bands. **Build:** Alt+D makes a linked duplicate (shares the mesh; edit one and they all change). For variation, rotate and scale copies, swap a material, or use Geometry Nodes to randomize rotation and scale. Use Shift+D when you want a copy you'll change.

name: fantasy maps and cartography (world maps, region maps, in-game maps) > Step 1: Believable geography
keywords: art blender fantasy map fantasy maps and cartography (world maps, region maps, in-game maps) Step 1: Believable geography guide path tutorial
text:
**You'll learn:** The rules readers subconsciously check:
- **Mountains** form in long ranges where tectonic plates collide, often near coasts. Single cone mountains are volcanoes.
- **Rivers** start in mountains and hills, flow downhill to the sea or a lake, and join as they go. They don't split on the way (except deltas at the sea), and they don't cross mountain ranges.
- **Rain shadow**: wind brings rain to one side of a range; the other side is dry (deserts sit behind mountains).
- **Biomes** follow latitude and rain: ice at the poles, forests in wet temperate areas, deserts around 30 degrees and in rain shadows, jungles at the wet equator.
- **Coastlines** are rough at every scale (the coastline paradox), so jagged, uneven coasts look real and smooth blobs don't.
- **Cities** sit on rivers, coasts and crossroads, because that's where trade and water are.
**Design question:** What story happens on this map? Put the important places first, then make the geography explain them (a fortress guards the only pass through the mountains).
**Done when:** You've sketched continents, ranges, rivers and the key places.
source: RusticEngine Blender Art Path 'art-blender-fantasy-map' step 1 (open it with game_path)

**You'll learn:** Generators are great for plausibility; the map becomes yours through your choices of places, names and style.
**Done when:** You have a base (generated or hand-drawn sketch).

keywords: art blender fantasy map fantasy maps and cartography (world maps, region maps, in-game maps) Step 4: Color by height (hypsometric tints) guide path tutorial
text:
**Build:** Terrain material: Texture Coordinate (Object) or Geometry > Position > Separate XYZ > Z > Map Range (sea level to highest peak into 0-1) > Color Ramp: sand, green lowlands, yellow-brown hills, gray rock, white peaks. Water: the sea plane colored deep blue, lighter near the coast (a Color Ramp on the terrain height just below 0 under transparent water).
**You'll learn:** **Hypsometric tints** (color by elevation) are a real cartography technique; atlases use them because readers understand height instantly.

name: fantasy maps and cartography (world maps, region maps, in-game maps) > Step 5: Hillshade and contour lines
keywords: art blender fantasy map fantasy maps and cartography (world maps, region maps, in-game maps) Step 5: Hillshade and contour lines guide path tutorial
text:
**Build:** Hillshade: a Sun light from the northwest (top left) at a low angle, Eevee rendering, so slopes facing it are bright and the others dark. Contour lines: Z height > Math Multiply (e.g. 20 = one line every 1/20 of the height range) > Math Fraction > Math Less Than 0.05 > use as a mix factor for thin dark lines over the color.
**You'll learn:** **Hillshading** from the top left is a cartography convention: light from the bottom right makes mountains read as valleys. **Contour lines** connect points of equal height; close lines mean steep ground.
**Done when:** Mountains pop out of the page.
source: RusticEngine Blender Art Path 'art-blender-fantasy-map' step 5 (open it with game_path)

keywords: art blender fantasy map fantasy maps and cartography (world maps, region maps, in-game maps) Step 6: Style it like a map guide path tutorial
text:
**Build:** Camera straight down (Numpad 7, then Ctrl+Alt+Numpad 0 to put the camera there), Orthographic. Parchment: mix a large soft Noise into the colors (Mix Multiply, low factor) and a darker vignette at the edges. Rivers, borders and roads: draw them with Grease Pencil (Shift+A > Grease Pencil > Blank, then Draw mode) or as curves with a thin bevel. Labels: Shift+A > Text, Tab to type, a serif or hand-lettered font, curved along a path for ranges and seas. Compass rose and cartouche (the title frame): model or draw them, or use CC0 assets.
**You'll learn:** Style choices: painted atlas, old parchment, clean modern. **Map symbols** (little mountain icons, tree clusters) are often clearer than realistic shading for a fantasy world map; you can mix both.

name: procedural texturing in Blender (wood, stone, rust, dirt, without painting a pixel) > Step 1: The Shader Editor
keywords: art blender procedural texturing procedural texturing in Blender (wood, stone, rust, dirt, without painting a pixel) Step 1: The Shader Editor guide path tutorial
text:
**Build:** Open the Shading workspace tab. Every material is a node graph that ends in Material Output. Shift+A adds nodes, drag between sockets to connect them, Ctrl+right-drag cuts links, M mutes a node, Ctrl+G groups nodes, Ctrl+H hides unused sockets, and Ctrl+Shift+click on any node previews its output in the viewport (the Viewer): use it constantly.
**You'll learn:** Nodes are a flow: coordinates in, patterns, then colors, then the shader. Read graphs left to right.
**Done when:** You can preview any node's output.
source: RusticEngine Blender Art Path 'art-blender-procedural-texturing' step 1 (open it with game_path)

name: procedural texturing in Blender (wood, stone, rust, dirt, without painting a pixel) > Step 2: Coordinates and noise
keywords: art blender procedural texturing procedural texturing in Blender (wood, stone, rust, dirt, without painting a pixel) Step 2: Coordinates and noise guide path tutorial
text:
**Build:** Texture Coordinate (Object or Generated) > Mapping > Noise Texture > Color Ramp > Base Color. Change Noise Scale, Detail, Roughness and watch. Stretch the noise with the Mapping node's Scale (e.g. X 1, Y 1, Z 20 = stretched along Z).
**You'll learn:** **Noise** is smooth randomness (Perlin noise, layered with fBM: more Detail adds finer layers). A **Color Ramp** turns the 0-1 noise values into colors or sharp masks. Stretched noise is already wood grain or brushed metal.
**Done when:** You've made brushed metal by stretching noise.
source: RusticEngine Blender Art Path 'art-blender-procedural-texturing' step 2 (open it with game_path)

name: procedural texturing in Blender (wood, stone, rust, dirt, without painting a pixel) > Step 3: Wood and stone
keywords: art blender procedural texturing procedural texturing in Blender (wood, stone, rust, dirt, without painting a pixel) Step 3: Wood and stone guide path tutorial
text:
**Build:** Grain: stretched Noise (Step 2) into a Color Ramp with two browns. Rings: Texture Coordinate (Object) > Separate XYZ > Combine XYZ using only X and Y (Z = 0) > Vector Math Length (distance from the trunk's center) > Math Multiply 20 (ring count) > Math Fraction (0-1 repeating) > Color Ramp (light to dark brown). Add a little noise to the coordinates before Separate XYZ (Vector Math Add) to make the rings wobble like real wood. Shortcut once you understand it: a Wave Texture set to Rings (Z axis, Distortion 3-5, Detail 3) does the same in one node. Stone: Voronoi Texture (F1) Color gives each stone its own shade; a second Voronoi set to Distance to Edge into a sharp Color Ramp draws the mortar and cracks; Brick Texture builds walls directly (Offset and Squash for irregular courses).
**You'll learn:** Most natural patterns are 1 base pattern + 1 distortion (add noise to the coordinates) + 1 color ramp.
**Done when:** It reads as wood (or stone) from a few meters away.
source: RusticEngine Blender Art Path 'art-blender-procedural-texturing' step 3 (open it with game_path)

name: procedural texturing in Blender (wood, stone, rust, dirt, without painting a pixel) > Step 4: Masks: dirt, rust, moss
keywords: art blender procedural texturing procedural texturing in Blender (wood, stone, rust, dirt, without painting a pixel) Step 4: Masks: dirt, rust, moss guide path tutorial
text:
**Build:** Build a mask (black/white) and use it as the Factor of a Mix node between two materials' colors (and roughness). Masks from: Noise with a sharp Color Ramp (patches), Geometry > Normal Z (up-facing surfaces: moss, snow, dust), Separate XYZ of Position Z (grime near the ground), Ambient Occlusion node (crevices: dirt).
**You'll learn:** Real wear follows logic: rust where water sits, moss on top, dirt in corners, wear on edges. Encode the logic, not random spots.
**Done when:** A crate has dirt in its corners and moss on top only.
source: RusticEngine Blender Art Path 'art-blender-procedural-texturing' step 4 (open it with game_path)

name: procedural texturing in Blender (wood, stone, rust, dirt, without painting a pixel) > Step 5: What survives into the game
keywords: art blender procedural texturing procedural texturing in Blender (wood, stone, rust, dirt, without painting a pixel) Step 5: What survives into the game guide path tutorial
text:
**You'll learn:** RusticEngine rebuilds: Principled BSDF, Image Texture, Noise (all five types: fBM, Multifractal, Hetero Terrain, Hybrid and Ridged, 2D/3D), Voronoi (every feature and distance, 2D/3D, with Detail), Wave, Brick, Magic, Checker, Gradient, White Noise, Mapping, Color Ramp, Math, Vector Math, Mix, RGB Curves, Map Range, Clamp, Separate/Combine, Bump, Normal Map, Texture Coordinate (UV, Object, Generated). Not yet: 1D/4D Noise and Voronoi (the W input), the Ambient Occlusion node, Geometry > Pointiness. Those materials come in plain (Ember can tell you exactly which node stopped it: ask about the .glb).
**Build:** Use asset_info on your exported .glb (or ask Ember "why does my crate look flat?") to see which materials were rebuilt. For the rest, bake (baking path) or swap the node for a supported one.
**Done when:** Your material shows as rebuilt in the import report, or is baked.

name: terrain and nature in Blender (landscapes, rivers, lakes, trees, grass) > Step 1: Plan the land
keywords: art blender terrain terrain and nature in Blender (landscapes, rivers, lakes, trees, grass) Step 1: Plan the land guide path tutorial
text:
**Design question:** What does the player do here, and where should their eye go? A landmark (mountain, tower, giant tree) visible from far away is how open worlds guide players without arrows.
**You'll learn:** Land follows rules: mountains form in ranges, valleys are cut by rivers, rivers flow downhill and join (they almost never split, except in deltas near the sea), lakes sit in low basins. Players feel when terrain breaks these rules.
**Done when:** You've sketched where the high ground, water and paths go.
source: RusticEngine Blender Art Path 'art-blender-terrain' step 1 (open it with game_path)

name: terrain and nature in Blender (landscapes, rivers, lakes, trees, grass) > Step 2: Make the ground
keywords: art blender terrain terrain and nature in Blender (landscapes, rivers, lakes, trees, grass) Step 2: Make the ground guide path tutorial
text:
**Build:** Shift+A > Mesh > Grid (e.g. 100 x 100 subdivisions, size 100 m), or the free A.N.T. Landscape extension (Get Extensions > search "A.N.T. Landscape") which generates noise landscapes with erosion settings. Shape it by hand in Sculpt Mode (Ctrl+Tab > Sculpt): G grab for big shapes, C clay strips to build up, S smooth, Ctrl+click to dig instead of raise, F to change brush size.
**You'll learn:** A **heightmap** is terrain stored as a grayscale image (white = high). Noise with several layers (fBM) looks like land because real terrain is self-similar: a rock looks like a small mountain. **Erosion** carves the believable details (valleys, ridges).
**Done when:** The big shapes match your plan when seen from the player's height.
source: RusticEngine Blender Art Path 'art-blender-terrain' step 2 (open it with game_path)

name: terrain and nature in Blender (landscapes, rivers, lakes, trees, grass) > Step 3: Rivers and lakes
keywords: art blender terrain terrain and nature in Blender (landscapes, rivers, lakes, trees, grass) Step 3: Rivers and lakes guide path tutorial
text:
**Build:** Carve the riverbed into the terrain (sculpt with Ctrl+drag, or a curve with a Shrinkwrap'd strip, then lower it). Rivers meander (curve back and forth) more on flat ground and run straight and fast in steep valleys. Add the water surfaces from the water path: a flat plane for the lake at one height, a strip for the river that steps down.
**You'll learn:** Water surfaces are always level across a lake; rivers drop in steps (rapids, falls) between level stretches. A lake with a sloped surface looks wrong instantly.
**Done when:** Water fits the ground with no floating or sunken edges.
source: RusticEngine Blender Art Path 'art-blender-terrain' step 3 (open it with game_path)

name: terrain and nature in Blender (landscapes, rivers, lakes, trees, grass) > Step 4: Ground materials
keywords: art blender terrain terrain and nature in Blender (landscapes, rivers, lakes, trees, grass) Step 4: Ground materials guide path tutorial
text:
**Build:** Blend materials by masks (procedural texturing path): rock on steep slopes (Geometry > Normal, Separate Z, Color Ramp: steep = rock), grass on flat ground, sand/mud near water (Position Z below a height), and paint the rest with a vertex color or painted mask. Free CC0 ground textures: Poly Haven and ambientCG (grass, rock, mud, forest floor).
**You'll learn:** Slope and height masks texture a whole landscape automatically, then hand painting adds paths and story. This is exactly how game engine terrain systems work too.
**Done when:** Rock, grass and sand fall where nature would put them.
source: RusticEngine Blender Art Path 'art-blender-terrain' step 4 (open it with game_path)

name: terrain and nature in Blender (landscapes, rivers, lakes, trees, grass) > Step 5: Trees and plants
keywords: art blender terrain terrain and nature in Blender (landscapes, rivers, lakes, trees, grass) Step 5: Trees and plants guide path tutorial
text:
**Build:** Free tree generators: Sapling Tree Gen (parametric trees with leaves, bones and wind) or Modular Tree (node-based), both in Get Extensions. IvyGen grows ivy over meshes. Make 3-5 tree variants, each low-poly with leaf cards (planes with a leaf texture with transparency). Free CC0 plant models: Poly Haven Models.
**You'll learn:** **L-systems** and branching rules make trees: each branch splits into smaller branches. Games use **leaf cards** (textured planes) instead of modeled leaves, and **LODs** (lower-detail versions far away), down to a flat **billboard** image at a distance.
**Done when:** You have a few tree variants with a sensible triangle count (game trees: 2,000-15,000 triangles).
source: RusticEngine Blender Art Path 'art-blender-terrain' step 5 (open it with game_path)

name: terrain and nature in Blender (landscapes, rivers, lakes, trees, grass) > Step 6: Scatter
keywords: art blender terrain terrain and nature in Blender (landscapes, rivers, lakes, trees, grass) Step 6: Scatter guide path tutorial
text:
**Build:** Geometry Nodes: on the terrain add a Geometry Nodes modifier, then Distribute Points on Faces (density by your grass mask) > Instance on Points (your grass clumps / rocks / trees from a collection, Pick Instance on) > Realize only if needed. Randomize rotation (Random Value into Rotation) and scale. Or the free Scatter Objects extension.
**You'll learn:** Scattering with masks (no trees on steep rock, grass thinning on paths) makes nature believable at scale. In the game, scattered copies should stay **instances**, not one giant mesh.
**Done when:** A forest edge looks natural, denser in valleys and thinner on slopes.

**Build:** Export the terrain mesh and the hero pieces (rocks, landmark trees) with Live Link. For big worlds, split the terrain into chunks (e.g. 64 x 64 m tiles) so the engine can stream and cull them.
**You'll learn:** Gameplay stays in RusticEngine (paths, colliders, spawn points) and is kept when you update terrain from Blender.

text:
**Build:** A camera looking at the origin at a fixed angle (e.g. 30 degrees down, 45 around), set to Orthographic in its properties. Output size square (Properties > Output: 256 x 256). Film > Transparent so the background is empty. Lights: one key light, one rim light behind, low ambient. Save this as icon_studio.blend.
**You'll learn:** **Three-point lighting** (key, fill, rim). The rim light separates the item from any background, which is what makes icons pop.

text:
**Build:** Outline: Properties > View Layer > enable Freestyle, or add a Solidify modifier with Flip Normals and a dark emission material (the "inverted hull" outline). Flat style: an Emission material with a Color Ramp (Constant) on light direction for a toon look.

keywords: art blender ui assets UI art with Blender (icons, item renders, frames and buttons) Step 5: Frames and buttons (9-slice) guide path tutorial
text:
**Build:** Model a frame (a beveled border around an empty middle), render it straight on with the ortho camera. In RusticEngine use it as a 9-slice: a StyleBoxTexture or NinePatchRect with margins equal to the border width, so the corners stay sharp at any size.
**You'll learn:** **9-slice scaling**: corners never stretch, edges stretch in one direction, the middle in both. One rendered frame then fits every window size.
**Done when:** One frame image fits a small tooltip and a big inventory window without distortion.

name: water and lava (stylized and realistic, for games) > Step 1: What makes water look like water
keywords: art blender water lava water and lava (stylized and realistic, for games) Step 1: What makes water look like water guide path tutorial
text:
**You'll learn:** Four things, in order of importance: **reflection** that gets stronger at grazing angles (Fresnel: look across a lake and it's a mirror; look down and you see through it), **transparency/depth color** (shallow water shows the bottom, deep water turns blue-green), **moving normals** (small waves only change lighting, not geometry), and **foam/edges** where water meets objects. Lava is the opposite: opaque, self-lit (emission) and slow.
**Done when:** You can point to each of the four in a reference photo or a game you like.
source: RusticEngine Blender Art Path 'art-blender-water-lava' step 1 (open it with game_path)

name: water and lava (stylized and realistic, for games) > Step 2: The water surface mesh
keywords: art blender water lava water and lava (stylized and realistic, for games) Step 2: The water surface mesh guide path tutorial
text:
**Build:** A plane for lakes and seas (Shift+A > Mesh > Plane), a curved strip for rivers (draw a Bezier curve along the riverbed, then a plane with Array + Curve modifiers to follow it, or extrude edges along the path). Subdivide only if the game will move vertices (big waves); otherwise keep it low-poly. UVs for rivers should run along the flow (U > Follow Active Quads on a quad strip), so the engine can scroll a texture downstream.
**You'll learn:** For rivers, the UV direction IS the flow direction. Waterfalls are just steep river strips.
**Done when:** You have a lake plane and a river strip with UVs running downstream.
source: RusticEngine Blender Art Path 'art-blender-water-lava' step 2 (open it with game_path)

name: water and lava (stylized and realistic, for games) > Step 3: Stylized water material
keywords: art blender water lava water and lava (stylized and realistic, for games) Step 3: Stylized water material guide path tutorial
text:
**Build:** Principled BSDF: Base Color deep blue-green, Roughness 0.05, Transmission 1 (or Alpha 0.6-0.8 with Blend Mode Alpha Blend in the material settings for the game). Waves: Noise Texture (Scale 5-20) > Bump node > Normal. Material Preview (Z) shows it.
**You'll learn:** In-game water usually uses alpha transparency rather than real refraction, because refraction is expensive. RusticEngine rebuilds the Noise + Bump; animated motion (scrolling the noise over time) is added in the engine's shader, since a Blender material doesn't know about game time. Ask Ember to make it flow.
**Done when:** The water reads as water in the viewport.
source: RusticEngine Blender Art Path 'art-blender-water-lava' step 3 (open it with game_path)

name: water and lava (stylized and realistic, for games) > Step 4: Shorelines and foam
keywords: art blender water lava water and lava (stylized and realistic, for games) Step 4: Shorelines and foam guide path tutorial
text:
**Build:** Foam where water meets land: paint a vertex color mask on the water mesh along the shores (Vertex Paint mode, white = foam) and mix a white color by it. In the game, foam can also come from depth (the engine can compare water depth to the ground behind it).
**You'll learn:** Shore foam and a darker depth color are what make stylized water look finished, even in very simple games.
**Done when:** The shoreline has a soft foam band.
source: RusticEngine Blender Art Path 'art-blender-water-lava' step 4 (open it with game_path)

name: water and lava (stylized and realistic, for games) > Step 5: Lava
keywords: art blender water lava water and lava (stylized and realistic, for games) Step 5: Lava guide path tutorial
text:
**Build:** Opaque, mostly Emission. Noise Texture (Detail 8) > Color Ramp from black (crust) through deep red and orange to yellow-white (hottest) > Emission Color, Emission Strength 2-10. Use the same ramp's dark part as Base Color with high Roughness for the cooled crust. Make cracks sharper by squeezing the Color Ramp stops together.
**You'll learn:** **Black-body radiation**: hot things glow from dark red through orange and yellow to white as they heat up. Lava colors follow that order, so the brightest parts are yellow-white, never pure red. Slow motion sells lava: it flows like honey, and the crust drifts.
**Done when:** It glows like the black-body color order.
source: RusticEngine Blender Art Path 'art-blender-water-lava' step 5 (open it with game_path)

name: water and lava (stylized and realistic, for games) > Step 6: Realistic oceans and simulations (for renders and reference)
keywords: art blender water lava water and lava (stylized and realistic, for games) Step 6: Realistic oceans and simulations (for renders and reference) guide path tutorial
text:
**Build:** Ocean modifier on a plane gives realistic wave shapes (and foam data), good for a still shoreline or a cinematic. Mantaflow (Physics > Fluid, a Domain plus a Flow object) simulates pouring, splashing liquid; bake it and render it for trailers, or study it as reference for timing.
**You'll learn:** Simulations are too heavy for gameplay. For a game, either bake a short simulation into a texture/flipbook or recreate the look with the shader approach above.
**Done when:** You know which of your liquids are shaders and which (if any) are pre-rendered effects.

name: a game-ready weapon in Blender (sword first, then axes, spears and maces) > Step 1: Design and references
keywords: art blender weapon a game-ready weapon in Blender (sword first, then axes, spears and maces) Step 1: Design and references guide path tutorial
text:
**Design question:** Who carries it, and what should it say about them? A knight's arming sword is plain and practical; a boss's greatsword exaggerates everything. How big is it next to the player? (A real longsword is about 1.1 m; one-handed arming swords are about 0.9 m; game weapons are often 10-20% oversized so they read on screen.)
**You'll learn:** The parts of a sword: blade (with an optional **fuller**, the groove that lightens it), **crossguard**, **grip** and **pommel**. Look up 'Longsword', 'Hilt' and 'Fuller' with blender_help for real references.
**Build:** Draw or collect a front and side picture (your concept art, or a photo of a real sword). In the RusticEngine sidebar tab press Add Reference Images, pick them and type the real length as the height. They line up by themselves. Look through them with Numpad 1 and 3.
**Done when:** You have the length, the silhouette and the parts decided.
source: RusticEngine Blender Art Path 'art-blender-weapon' step 1 (open it with game_path)

name: a game-ready weapon in Blender (sword first, then axes, spears and maces) > Step 2: Block out with primitives
keywords: art blender weapon a game-ready weapon in Blender (sword first, then axes, spears and maces) Step 2: Block out with primitives guide path tutorial
text:
**Build:** One object per part: a cube scaled flat for the blade (S X 0.03, S Y 0.008 with real numbers), a cube for the guard, a cylinder (8-12 sides) for the grip, a UV sphere or cylinder for the pommel. Shift+D duplicates, Ctrl+A > Scale applies scale on each part.
**You'll learn:** **Silhouette first.** At game distance players only see the outline. Check it in front view with the shading pie (Z) set to solid and the overlays off (Shift+Alt+Z): does it read as YOUR weapon in black?
**Done when:** The gray blockout matches the reference outline in front and side views.
source: RusticEngine Blender Art Path 'art-blender-weapon' step 2 (open it with game_path)

name: a game-ready weapon in Blender (sword first, then axes, spears and maces) > Step 3: Shape the blade
keywords: art blender weapon a game-ready weapon in Blender (sword first, then axes, spears and maces) Step 3: Shape the blade guide path tutorial
text:
**Build:** Tab into the blade. Ctrl+R adds loops along the length. Select the tip vertices and merge them (M > At Center) for the point, or scale them on X (S X 0) for a chisel tip. For the edge bevel (the sharpened sides), select the two long side edges and scale them on Y (S Y 0) so the cross-section becomes a diamond. Add a Mirror modifier on X and Y if the blade is symmetrical, with Clipping on.
**You'll learn:** A blade's cross-section (diamond, lenticular, hollow-ground) is what makes light run along it. Low-poly blades need only 1-2 loops across; spend the vertices on the silhouette.
**Try it yourself:** A fuller: inset (I) a long thin strip of faces on the flat of the blade, then extrude it inward (E, -0.002).
**Done when:** The blade catches light along its edge in Material Preview (Z).

keywords: art blender weapon a game-ready weapon in Blender (sword first, then axes, spears and maces) Step 4: Guard, grip and pommel guide path tutorial
text:
**Build:** Guard: extrude (E) the ends of the guard cube and scale them to flare, or bevel (Ctrl+B, scroll for segments) for a rounded bar. Grip: loop-cut (Ctrl+R) the cylinder 6-10 times and scale alternate loops (Alt+click, S) for wrapped leather ridges. Pommel: a low-poly sphere scaled flat, or a cylinder beveled.
**You'll learn:** **Weld points**: parts may intersect each other instead of being joined; games don't care about hidden intersections, and separate parts are easier to texture. Join them at the end with Ctrl+J.
**Done when:** All four parts are in place and the whole thing still reads in silhouette.

name: a game-ready weapon in Blender (sword first, then axes, spears and maces) > Step 5: Clean shading
keywords: art blender weapon a game-ready weapon in Blender (sword first, then axes, spears and maces) Step 5: Clean shading guide path tutorial
text:
**Build:** Add a Bevel modifier (Amount ~2 mm, Segments 2, Limit Method Angle) and a Weighted Normal modifier (turn on Keep Sharp), or use Object > Shade Auto Smooth. Check with Z > Material Preview.
**You'll learn:** Small bevels plus weighted normals make low-poly hard surfaces look high quality without a baked normal map. Watch the triangle count in the status bar (right-click it > Scene Statistics): a hero weapon in a modern game is 2,000-10,000 triangles; stylized ones 300-2,000.
**Done when:** No dark smudges on flat faces, and edges catch a highlight.

name: a game-ready weapon in Blender (sword first, then axes, spears and maces) > Step 6: UV unwrap
keywords: art blender weapon a game-ready weapon in Blender (sword first, then axes, spears and maces) Step 6: UV unwrap guide path tutorial
text:
**Build:** Mark seams where you'd cut the surface open to lay it flat: select edges, Ctrl+E > Mark Seam (along the blade's edges, around the grip, under the guard). Select all (A), U > Unwrap. Look at it in the UV Editing workspace tab. Give the material an image of the UV grid (Image Texture > New > Generated Type: UV Grid) to see stretching.
**You'll learn:** UVs map the 3D surface onto a 2D picture. Seams are cuts; hide them where players won't look. **Texel density**: every part should get roughly the same pixels per meter, or one part looks blurry next to another (the free Texel Density Checker extension measures it). Symmetrical parts can overlap in UV space to save texture room.
**Done when:** The checker squares are square and about the same size everywhere.

name: a game-ready weapon in Blender (sword first, then axes, spears and maces) > Step 7: Materials and texture
keywords: art blender weapon a game-ready weapon in Blender (sword first, then axes, spears and maces) Step 7: Materials and texture guide path tutorial
text:
**Build:** Separate materials for steel, leather and wood/brass, each a Principled BSDF: steel Metallic 1, Roughness 0.3-0.4; leather Roughness 0.7 with a Noise Texture into a Color Ramp for variation. RusticEngine rebuilds Noise, Checker, Gradient, Color Ramp, Math and Mix nodes as real shaders. Free CC0 metal and leather texture sets are on Poly Haven and ambientCG (ask Ember for one). For painted detail, use Texture Paint mode or follow the baking path.
**You'll learn:** **PBR**: base color, metallic, roughness and normal describe what the surface is, so it looks right under any light. Metal has no diffuse color; its color is in its reflections.
**Done when:** It looks like steel and leather in Material Preview, not plastic.

keywords: art blender weapon a game-ready weapon in Blender (sword first, then axes, spears and maces) Step 8: Ready for the game guide path tutorial
text:
**Build:** Put the origin where the hand holds it (select the grip's center in Edit Mode, Shift+S > Cursor to Selected, then in Object Mode Object > Set Origin > Origin to 3D Cursor). Point the blade along a consistent axis (e.g. +Y). Name it (F2). Export with Live Link on.
**You'll learn:** The origin is the attachment point: the engine attaches a weapon to the hand bone at the origin. A consistent orientation lets every weapon swap into the same socket.
**Done when:** The sword shows up in RusticEngine, and attaching it to a hand needs no rotation fixes.
